Create a Function that Validates and Transforms Caller Arguments

Source: R/make_arg_validator.R
make_arg_validator.Rd

make_arg_validator() is a function factory: it takes an unquoted expression written in terms of argument names and returns a validator function. When that validator is called from inside another function, it captures the calling function's arguments, evaluates the expression against them, and returns the (possibly checked or coerced) arguments as a named list.

This keeps argument checking and normalization out of the body of the function that uses them, and lets several functions share a single set of rules.

Usage

make_arg_validator(expr)

Arguments

expr

An unquoted R expression, usually a { ... } block. Symbols in the expression are resolved against the caller's arguments, and assignments inside the expression update those arguments. The expression is evaluated in a child of the calling frame of the validator, so ordinary lexical scoping applies: helpers, constants and attached packages visible from the caller remain visible, while package functions should be called with ::. The caller's ... is forwarded to that environment as well, so dots helpers such as rlang::check_dots_empty(), ...length() or ..1 behave exactly as they would in the calling function.

Value

make_arg_validator() returns a validator: a function with a single argument, env, which defaults to rlang::caller_env(), i.e. the environment of the function that called the validator.

Calling the validator forces every promise bound in env (so lazy default values are evaluated), evaluates expr against those bindings, and returns a named list of the objects bound in env, ordered by name. Values reassigned by expr replace the originals; the caller's own bindings are never modified in place.

Details

What gets captured

The validator copies every object in the caller's own evaluation frame (inherits = FALSE). As a consequence:

  • local temporaries created before the validator is called are captured too, not only the formal arguments. Filter the result if you want the formals only, for example with filter_args_for_func() from standalone-args_to_func.R.

  • objects from enclosing scopes (the global environment, an outer function, the package namespace) are not part of the result, even though expr can still read them.

  • ... is never part of the result, because a dots object cannot be stored in a list. It is still forwarded to the environment expr runs in, so list(...), ...length(), ...elt(), ..1 and rlang::check_dots_empty() all behave as they do inside the calling function.

What gets returned

Only names that already exist in env are kept, so a variable that expr creates from scratch is dropped: the validator updates arguments, it does not add them. The updates reach the caller exclusively through the returned list. The two common patterns are therefore args <- validate_x(); args$a for a one-off value, and list2env(validate_x(), envir = environment()) to write everything back into the calling frame.

Errors

Errors signalled by expr propagate to the caller unchanged, so classed conditions can be caught with tryCatch(). An argument without a default that was never supplied fails with "argument \"x\" is missing, with no default" when its promise is forced by the capture step.

Supplying env explicitly

Passing env bypasses the caller lookup and validates the given environment instead, which is convenient for validating a list of options, a config object, or a shiny session environment.

Examples


# ---- 1. Check the arguments, then use the validated values ---------------
validate_add <- make_arg_validator({
  if (!is.numeric(x) || length(x) != 1L) {
    rlang::abort("`x` must be a single number.", call = NULL)
  }
  if (!is.numeric(y) || length(y) != 1L) {
    rlang::abort("`y` must be a single number.", call = NULL)
  }
})

add <- function(x, y) {
  args <- validate_add()
  args$x + args$y
}

add(1, 2)
#> [1] 3
#> [1] 3

# validation errors keep their message and reach the caller unchanged
tryCatch(add("a", 2), error = function(cnd) conditionMessage(cnd))
#> [1] "`x` must be a single number."
#> [1] "`x` must be a single number."

# ---- 2. Coerce first, write the result back into the calling frame -------
validate_ratio <- make_arg_validator({
  numerator <- as.numeric(numerator)
  denominator <- as.numeric(denominator)
  if (denominator == 0) {
    rlang::abort("`denominator` must not be zero.", call = NULL)
  }
})

ratio <- function(numerator, denominator) {
  list2env(validate_ratio(), envir = environment())
  numerator / denominator
}

ratio("3", 2)
#> [1] 1.5
#> [1] 1.5

tryCatch(ratio(1, 0), error = function(cnd) conditionMessage(cnd))
#> [1] "`denominator` must not be zero."
#> [1] "`denominator` must not be zero."

# ---- 3. Share one validator between several functions --------------------
validate_draw <- make_arg_validator({
  color <- match.arg(color, c("red", "green", "blue"))
  size <- max(size, 1)
})

draw_point <- function(x, y, color = "red", size = 0) {
  args <- validate_draw()
  sprintf(
    "point (%s, %s) color=%s size=%s", x, y, args$color, args$size
  )
}

draw_point(1, 2, color = "green", size = 0)
#> [1] "point (1, 2) color=green size=1"
#> [1] "point (1, 2) color=green size=1"

# ---- 4. Only bindings that already existed are returned ------------------
validate_scale <- make_arg_validator({
  span <- max(x) - min(x)
  x <- (x - min(x)) / span
})

scale01 <- function(x) validate_scale()

scale01(c(0, 5, 10))
#> $x
#> [1] 0.0 0.5 1.0
#> 
#> $x
#> [1] 0.0 0.5 1.0
# `span` was created inside the expression, so it is not part of the result

# ---- 5. Validate an environment directly ---------------------------------
validate_opts <- make_arg_validator({
  name <- trimws(name)
  threads <- as.integer(threads)
})

opts <- list2env(list(name = "  model  ", threads = "4"))
validate_opts(opts)
#> $name
#> [1] "model"
#> 
#> $threads
#> [1] 4
#> 
#> $name
#> [1] "model"
#>
#> $threads
#> [1] 4

# ---- 6. Local temporaries are captured as well ---------------------------
validate_pos <- make_arg_validator({
  if (x <= 0) {
    rlang::abort("`x` must be positive.", call = NULL)
  }
})

sqrt_checked <- function(x) {
  tmp <- "not an argument"
  args <- validate_pos()
  names(args)
}

sqrt_checked(4)
#> [1] "tmp" "x"  
#> [1] "tmp" "x"

# ---- 7. Classed conditions can be caught ---------------------------------
validate_n <- make_arg_validator({
  if (!is.numeric(n)) {
    rlang::abort(
      "`n` must be numeric.",
      class = "rpkgkit_bad_n",
      call = NULL
    )
  }
})

count_up <- function(n) validate_n()

tryCatch(
  count_up("a"),
  rpkgkit_bad_n = function(cnd) "caught a classed error"
)
#> [1] "caught a classed error"
#> [1] "caught a classed error"

# ---- 8. `...` is forwarded to `expr` but never returned ------------------
validate_no_dots <- make_arg_validator({
  rlang::check_dots_empty()
})

strict <- function(x, ...) validate_no_dots()

strict(1)
#> $x
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $x
#> [1] 1

# the dots check sees the caller's `...`, not an empty environment
tryCatch(strict(1, 2), rlib_error_dots_nonempty = function(cnd) "dots seen")
#> [1] "dots seen"
#> [1] "dots seen"

validate_dots <- make_arg_validator({
  if (...length() > 2L) {
    rlang::abort("at most two values are supported.", call = NULL)
  }
})

pick <- function(x, ...) validate_dots()

tryCatch(pick(1, 2, 3, 4), error = function(cnd) conditionMessage(cnd))
#> [1] "at most two values are supported."
#> [1] "at most two values are supported."
